title: Lecture 10 - Storage engines: a word dictionary without a database, and a super fast key-value store on disk (Bitcask)

questions.q: What two problems were on the agenda for this session?
questions.answer: (1) Building a word dictionary without using any (traditional) database; (2) building a super fast key-value store.

questions.q: In the word-dictionary problem, which kinds of systems were ruled out, and what two non-functional requirements were set (one relaxed, one demanded)?
questions.answer: No traditional database at all: no MySQL, Postgres, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch, Memcache. Response time is allowed to be high (performance tricks like caching are known and not the focus), but the solution must be portable. It must still be scalable on both storage and API servers.

questions.q: How do words and meanings get updated in the dictionary problem?
questions.answer: Only weekly (e.g. every Sunday) through a changelog file containing the updated words and meanings; there are no live pointed updates. The changelog must be applied to whatever storage you build. The dictionary is otherwise read-only/read-heavy.

questions.q: What is the lookup contract of the dictionary, and what are its size numbers?
questions.answer: Lookup is always a single word (no autocomplete): given a word, return its meaning, or 404 if it does not exist. The dictionary is 1 TB big and has 170,000 words.

questions.q: What four axes did the teacher list to brainstorm the dictionary on?
questions.answer: Storage, querying, portability, seamless updates.

questions.q: Why was a single JSON file containing all words and meanings rejected?
questions.answer: To check whether one word exists you must read the entire JSON file, deserialize it and build an in-memory object/hash map first; there is no direct way to access one item without reading the whole file. With a 1 TB file that is far too costly.

questions.q: What was the first text-file format drawn for the dictionary?
questions.answer: A CSV-style text file: one line per word, key then comma then meaning, e.g. `apple, a fruit` / `amazon, a rainforest`, each line ending with a newline.

questions.q: What constraint did the teacher add about duplicates, and why?
questions.answer: No repetitive entries: each word appears only once in the file. Portability means someone could open the file in any text editor; duplicates would make it hard to use.

questions.q: When first asked whether the text file should be kept sorted, what did the student answer and why?
questions.answer: No sorting: since response time is allowed to be high there was no need to keep the words in any order; words could come in any order.

questions.q: How read-heavy did the class agree the dictionary is?
questions.answer: Very read-heavy; a student suggested a 1000:1 read:write ratio and the teacher said it is much more skewed than that.

questions.q: A student said each single-word update must not be costly. How did the teacher qualify this given the weekly updates?
questions.answer: He agreed a single word update should not be costly, but since updates arrive in a weekly batch, it is acceptable to do one huge processing job for the batch.

questions.q: Why did the teacher reject splitting the dictionary into many partitioned files (even when bundled into one zip)?
questions.answer: Multiple files kill portability: the goal is one single file that can be copied and shipped and read directly. A zip of many folders still has to be extracted before use. He said this constraint forms the foundation for many systems discussed later.

questions.q: What real AWS feature was the dictionary design trying to simulate, and why keep it simple instead of Parquet/Avro/Lucene?
questions.answer: Uploading a plain CSV file to S3 and querying it with Athena; the class was simulating how such an engine would be built. He kept it simple (no Parquet/B+ trees) to build the base concepts first; those formats are a later level.

questions.q: When a student started on B+ trees, blocks and pages, what did the teacher say?
questions.answer: That it is over-engineering for a simple word dictionary; keep it very simple (no B+ trees or anything fancy), because simplicity is where the power and beauty of the system show.

questions.q: Describe the naive lookup on the CSV file and its cost per request.
questions.answer: Open the file, read it line by line until the key is found, then stop and return the meaning. That is a linear scan: worst case you read the whole 1 TB per request, on average about half (0.5 TB = 500 GB).

questions.q: Besides slowness, what other problems did the teacher name for linear scanning a 1 TB file on every read?
questions.answer: It degrades disk performance and the disk sectors go bad from heavy over-utilization: hardware problems, software problems and time problems.

questions.q: What did the teacher say should always come to mind when reads are slow?
questions.answer: Indexing.

questions.q: What does each entry of the one-level index contain, and what exactly is the offset?
questions.answer: The key (word) and an offset; the offset is the byte position (nth byte from the start of the data file) where that word's line starts. Drawn as `apple, o1` / `amazon, o2` / `book, o3`, each with an arrow to its line in the data file.

questions.q: Even if you scan the index file linearly, why is that much better than scanning the data file?
questions.answer: The data file's lines carry huge meanings (MBs of data), while each index entry is just the word plus a 4-byte offset, so the index is tiny and fast to read sequentially; then you do one pointed read in the data file.

questions.q: A student proposed an index of just 26 entries (one per letter A-Z). What was wrong with it?
questions.answer: You would still have to scan all words under that letter to find the one word; an index with the exact offset per word lets you go directly to the line. And the full per-word index turns out small enough to fit in memory anyway.

questions.q: What formula and components were used to estimate the size of one index record?
questions.answer: Average English word length about 4.3 bytes + 4 bytes for the integer offset + 2 bytes (one comma, one newline) = 10.3 bytes per entry; total = 170,000 x (4.3 + 4 + 2).

questions.q: What did the index size come out to, and what was the conclusion?
questions.answer: 10.3 x 170,000 = 1,751,000 bytes = 1751 KB = about 1.751 MB (1.75 MB). That is peanuts: the index easily fits in RAM, so load it into an in-memory hash map.

questions.q: What general lesson did the teacher draw from the index-size calculation?
questions.answer: Number crunching is very important in design: what looks huge (a 1 TB file, 170,000 words) gives an index of under 2 MB, so a simple one-level in-memory index suffices instead of over-complicated schemes (like A-Z partitioning).

questions.q: With the index in memory, what is the lookup flow on the API server?
questions.answer: Load the index into an in-memory hash table when the server starts; on a request, look up the word in the hash table to get the offset, go to that offset in the data file, read the line (meaning) and return it. No linear scan, just a pointed read.

questions.q: After indexing, what two files existed and why was that a problem?
questions.answer: `index.dict` (the index) and `data.dict` (the data). Shipping the dictionary now means two files, which breaks the portability requirement of a single file.

questions.q: Why not drop the index file and rebuild the index in memory at every startup?
questions.answer: That means iterating through the whole 1 TB data file at every startup, which is avoidable: the data only changes once a week, so the index can be precomputed and stored.

questions.q: When the index and data are concatenated into one file, what question arises, and what were the first two options proposed?
questions.answer: How do you know where the index ends and the data begins? (1) A special line / separator between them; (2) pre-allocate a fixed size for the index (e.g. the first 2 MB), since the index is ~1.75 MB and grows slowly.

questions.q: What did the teacher think of the fixed-size (2 MB) index region?
questions.answer: A nice hack that works (the reader knows the first 2 MB is index), but it wastes some space; he asked to be more frugal.

questions.q: A student proposed growing data from the top and the index from the bottom of the file like a stack. What objection was raised?
questions.answer: You still must know where one ends and the other begins (when to stop reading the index); once they meet you need a separator anyway, and meanwhile the gap between them is wasted space.

questions.q: What improvement over a separator did the teacher suggest storing at the start of the file, and what is the general name of this idea?
questions.answer: Store the byte offset where the data begins (or equivalently the index size) at the beginning of the file. This is a file header: a fixed-size first chunk holding meta information about the file's sections, used by every file format (PNG, JPG, MP3, AVI, ...).

questions.q: List the fields of the dictionary file header in order, with their sizes and the total.
questions.answer: Format name / magic bytes (e.g. OUR_DICT) - 8 bytes; version - 4 bytes; index size - 4 bytes. Total: a fixed 16-byte header.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the magic-name bytes and of the version field in the header?
questions.answer: The first bytes tell the decoder what format the file is (like PNG's first bytes; the teacher's example name was AODB, 'Arpit's outstanding database'). The version lets the layout vary between variants (e.g. v1 index then data, v2 data then index) so the decoder knows how to read it.

questions.q: Describe how the server reads the single-file dictionary at boot, step by step.
questions.answer: Read the first 16 bytes (fixed header): first 8 bytes = it is our dictionary, next 4 = version, next 4 = index size. Then read that many bytes after the header as the index and build an in-memory hash table. Everything after that is data, which the index offsets point into.

questions.q: How did the teacher relate the header/sections idea to formats like MP4?
questions.answer: A custom file format creates compartments (sections) in one file plus a header that says where each compartment lies. In MP4 the sections are the video part (frames) and the audio part (waveform); in the dictionary they are index and data.

questions.q: Why must a JSON file be read in full, while a format like Parquet need not?
questions.answer: JSON (and CSV) are plain text formats without a header; the JSON decoder must parse braces, quotes and strings of the whole file to build the in-memory dictionary. Formats like Parquet, PDF and PPT have headers/meta information describing where things are.

questions.q: What does an encoder and a decoder do for a file format, and what does 'this browser does not support TIF' mean?
questions.answer: The encoder creates a file in the specific format; the decoder interprets the bytes. 'Does not support TIF' means the browser has no decoder for that format, so it does not know how to interpret the bytes. Our decoder knows: 16 bytes header -> index size -> index -> data.

questions.q: Draw the final layout of the portable dictionary file from left to right.
questions.answer: One long file: header (small, fixed 16 bytes, at the left), then the index section, then the data section (the large rest). The header stores the index size / byte offset of the data. Labelled 'Portable'.

questions.q: What is the request path for serving the dictionary as first drawn?
questions.answer: User sends `GET /word` -> load balancer -> one of several API servers, which must find the meaning in the dictionary file and return it.

questions.q: What three objections were raised to keeping a copy of the dictionary file on every API server, and which one did the teacher call the biggest?
questions.answer: Updates become tedious, data inconsistency if an update partially fails (acceptable since meanings change little), and cost. Cost is the biggest pain: duplicating 1 TB on SSDs on every server, e.g. 100 servers = 100 TB of redundant data.

questions.q: What principle about cost did the teacher state, using the 'put everything in RAM' example?
questions.answer: Real-world system design is doing the bare minimum at the bare minimum cost; if you don't think about cost you aren't building good systems. You could load the whole 1 TB dictionary into RAM on each machine and skip the index, but that is not cost effective, so not a good solution.

questions.q: Why must the shared dictionary storage be something accessible over the network?
questions.answer: Because we refuse to replicate the file to every server (cost), it must sit in a central place, and the only thing common to multiple servers is the network. Since databases are disallowed, use a block/blob storage such as S3, still keeping the one portable file.

questions.q: What S3 feature did a student point out that makes the design work?
questions.answer: S3 GetObject accepts a byte range, so you can read only specific bytes: read the header/index bytes, then read just the bytes at an entry's offset to return a meaning. (Cheap, optimized for blobs.)

questions.q: What is the minimum capability the central storage must provide, and how was it written on the board?
questions.answer: Network attached storage with file system semantics, specifically random reads: given (file, offset, n), read n bytes from that offset - like a seek then read on a normal disk.

questions.q: Name alternatives to S3 that satisfy the requirement, and why S3 was chosen in class.
questions.answer: HDFS (same semantics) or literal network hard disks in your data center (e.g. Dell network disks) - anything with file-system-level semantics. S3 was chosen only because everyone understands it, not as a preference.

questions.q: What does each API server need to know at startup, and what S3 calls does it make before serving?
questions.answer: The dictionary's file path on S3 (initially static configuration). It reads the first 16 bytes (header) to get the index size, makes another S3 call to read that many bytes (the index), and builds the in-memory hash table (word -> offset).

questions.q: How is a GET for a word served once the server is up?
questions.answer: Check the in-memory hash table: if the word is absent return 404; if present, take its offset and do a ranged (random) read on S3 of just those bytes, then return the meaning - nothing before, nothing after.

questions.q: What did the teacher call 'magical' about what had been built by this point?
questions.answer: The ability to make pointed reads on S3: read one specific record without reading the whole file. Effectively a key-value store (a database) supporting huge numbers of GETs on S3.

questions.q: Where does the weekly update job run and what does it start with?
questions.answer: On a separate server spun up for the job (periodic/cron-like, triggered when Oxford's update arrives). It downloads the dictionary from S3 and has the changelog (only the changes, not the whole dictionary).

questions.q: Why was 'append the changelog entries at the end of the dictionary' rejected?
questions.answer: The dictionary would grow forever and contain duplicate entries, violating the no-repetitive-entries requirement.

questions.q: Why did the teacher say hashing/diffing the old and new entries was unnecessary?
questions.answer: The changelog already contains exactly what must change, so no hash comparison or diff generation is needed. 'It's easy to build complex systems; it's very difficult to build simple systems.'

questions.q: What happens if you use the index offset to overwrite 'apple, a fruit' in place with 'apple, a round fruit'?
questions.answer: On disk, writing at an offset blindly overwrites bytes; it does not push later lines down like an editor in memory. The longer new meaning spills over and corrupts the next entry ('ball, a round obj').

questions.q: What three hats did the teacher say a good engineer wears, and which one exposes the overwrite problem?
questions.answer: Product manager, architect and engineer. The engineer hat - thinking about the actual code you would write - reveals what breaks.

questions.q: Why was 'append a new version and compact later' (tombstone-style) rejected for the dictionary?
questions.answer: It violates no repetitive entries, and that approach suits live updates; with a once-a-week batch update you can do a clean rebuild directly.

questions.q: What approach to applying the changelog did the teacher endorse, and what classic algorithm is it?
questions.answer: Create a new file by walking the existing dictionary and the changelog together, writing entries in order with updates applied: the merge step of merge sort (merging two sorted lists/arrays into a third). It is the best approach, not a naive one.

questions.q: What precondition makes the merge efficient, and what if the changelog is not sorted?
questions.answer: Both files must be sorted by word. The changelog is small, so if it is not sorted, load it in memory, sort it and dump it.

questions.q: In the board's merge example, the dictionary holds a-a', b-b', c-c', d-d', f-f', g-g', h-h' and the changelog holds c-c'', e-e', f-f''. What is the new dictionary?
questions.answer: a-a', b-b', c-c'', d-d', e-e', f-f'', g-g', h-h'. On equal keys the changelog's updated meaning wins and both pointers advance; the smaller key is written otherwise; once the changelog is exhausted the rest of the dictionary is copied.

questions.q: How does this merge differ from merging two arrays in memory?
questions.answer: You do not load the 1 TB dictionary into memory; you iterate both files line by line with two pointers and write a third file. You always write new entries to a new file because writing in place would overwrite the next line.

questions.q: What disk-size constraint does the merge job impose on the update server?
questions.answer: Its disk must be at least 2 TB: the 1 TB old dictionary plus the 1 TB new one. Acceptable because it is just one server.

questions.q: What concern about deployment did a student raise if the new file is uploaded to the same S3 path?
questions.answer: Rollback: if the upload fails or the file gets corrupted in transit you must detect it and fall back to the previous file; so stage it in temporary storage, verify, then mark it successful.

questions.q: Using the board's example 'apple: 100, 1024', explain why uploading the new file to the same S3 path serves garbage.
questions.answer: API servers already hold the old index in memory (apple at offset 100, 1024 bytes). After the new file replaces the old one at the same path, offsets have shifted; reading 1024 bytes at offset 100 returns some other word, possibly from its middle. Until every server reloads its index, users see garbage.

questions.q: Besides garbage reads, what other problems did same-path upload have?
questions.answer: What if the upload fails, or the file is corrupted - you overwrite the good version; and you still must tell every server to reload its index.

questions.q: What upload scheme was chosen instead, and what question does it leave?
questions.answer: Upload each new dictionary to a new path, e.g. s3://wd/dict1.dict then s3://wd/dict2.dict. It leaves the question of how to tell the API servers the new path to start serving.

questions.q: Why were 'ping every API server to invalidate its cache' and 'have servers switch at the known job time' rejected?
questions.answer: Pinging all servers is too complex. A time-based switch (e.g. Sunday 1 PM everyone updates) is unreliable: the job may run late, the upload may fail, the file may be corrupt or unvalidated, yet servers switch anyway.

questions.q: What was wrong with storing one file per word on S3 (a folder per first letter)?
questions.answer: It breaks the major requirement of portability.

questions.q: Describe the metadata-file proposal. Must the meta file's own path be static or versioned?
questions.answer: Keep a small meta file (meta.json, e.g. `{ path: "..." }`) on S3 holding the current dictionary path; after a successful upload, update it. Its own path is static so every server knows where to look. API servers poll it (e.g. every 5-10 minutes) and reload the index from the new path when it changes.

questions.q: Why would you poll every few minutes if the job runs weekly, according to the student?
questions.answer: You can't know exactly when the new file lands: e.g. updates arrive Sunday but S3 is down, so the upload happens Monday; servers would not know unless they keep polling.

questions.q: How can polling be replaced reactively, and what drawback did the teacher see in that?
questions.answer: Redis Pub/Sub: all API servers subscribe; the update server publishes an event when the upload is done, so servers reload instead of polling thousands of times a week. Drawback: another infrastructure component to run and every API server holding a persistent connection - too complex.

questions.q: Why were 'a latest flag in the header' and 'check the version on each request' rejected?
questions.answer: You cannot know something changed without polling: a latest flag still has to be polled, and checking a version/updated-at on every request is still polling and adds an expensive extra meta call per request (and reading the changed data file would already give garbage).

questions.q: Was the teacher against polling in principle?
questions.answer: No. Polling is fine; the point is why make ~5,000 requests when someone can tell you or trigger something.

questions.q: In the prepared 'Transitions' notes, what three transition strategies were listed, and what does the periodic-refresh timeline show?
questions.answer: 1. Periodic refresh of the server's index (pull at intervals; between the index.dat change on S3 and the next pull, responses are garbage; graceful termination/reload); 2. Reactive: Pub/Sub (Redis pipe to the API boxes, a standalone updater publishing); 3. Parallel setup.

questions.q: What hint did the teacher give to converge on the simplest reload mechanism?
questions.answer: On boot an API server already reads meta.json, gets the path, reads the dictionary, builds the index and serves. So after updating meta.json you just need to trigger a reload of the server - equivalent to a boot.

questions.q: How did the teacher relate S3 object versioning to the meta-file design?
questions.answer: It is the same idea: different files plus a meta file saying which one is active/latest; S3 versioning can abstract that, but he laid it out in simple terms.

questions.q: What was the final mechanism to make API servers serve the new dictionary?
questions.answer: After uploading the new file to a new path and updating meta.json, the update server triggers a deployment (via AWS SDK / deployment pipeline / Jenkins job). A rolling deployment replaces servers one by one; each new server boots, reads meta.json, gets the new path, builds the index and serves. No Pub/Sub, endpoints or polling needed.

questions.q: What inconsistency occurs during the rolling deployment, and why is it acceptable?
questions.answer: For a while some requests hit old servers (old index on old file) and some hit new servers (new data) - eventually consistent. Acceptable because meanings don't change drastically and no one gets garbage, since each server's index matches the file it reads.

questions.q: On the board's update diagram, what does the purple 'Deploy' arrow connect?
questions.answer: From `AWS SDK` at the update server up to the load balancer / API servers (the Pub/Sub pipe was erased and replaced by this).

questions.q: In what order must the update job do its final steps?
questions.answer: Create the new merged file (with new header and index) and upload it to a new path, then update meta.json, and only then trigger the API servers' deployment.

questions.q: What does the prepared 'Updating the dictionary' procedure list, step by step?
questions.answer: Spin up a new server; download the dictionary locally; download the changelog; merge in O(n), creating a new dictionary and index locally; upload the new dictionary and index to S3. Merge is O(n) because dictionary and index are sorted: merging two sorted lists.

questions.q: Using Amazon orders, explain multi-tiered storage enabled by pointed reads on S3.
questions.answer: Old orders (e.g. older than six months) are rarely accessed, so move them to S3 while recent orders stay in the hot DB (MySQL). Users can still look up old orders: recent -> MySQL, old -> pointed read on S3 by order ID. You keep the ability to query the data you dumped on S3.

questions.q: What is the trade-off of moving data to S3 cold storage, and why is it worth it?
questions.answer: You trade latency: S3 reads are relatively slow vs. the hot DB. Since the data is infrequently accessed that is okay, and moving it out of the hot database significantly cuts the hot database's cost. S3 is not just archival here.

questions.q: Which real systems did the teacher say do essentially the same thing as the S3 dictionary?
questions.answer: Athena (load a CSV on S3, it builds/keeps an index and reads the records on query), data lakes (huge data in cheap storage yet queryable), Apache Hudi (its table format is this kind of index) and Hive partitions.

questions.q: What alternatives to redeployment did the teacher acknowledge, and why did he still prefer triggering a deployment?
questions.answer: Expose API endpoints that tell servers to reload the new file (reactive), or even push the ~1.7 MB index itself to servers so nothing has to be reloaded. He chose deployment because it is an out-of-the-box approach many engineers don't consider: cost is the same and it avoids polling, Pub/Sub and custom code - we control our infrastructure.

questions.q: What did the teacher promise the second half (after the break) would deliver?
questions.answer: A super fast key-value store with O(1) reads, writes and deletes with persistence, getting the max performance out of a (cheap) hard disk, with a real record file format instead of CSV - a database 'everyone uses unknowingly'.

questions.q: What are the requirements of the super fast KV store and on what hardware?
questions.answer: Superfast reads, writes (updates), deletes, plus persistence, on cheap commodity magnetic hard disks.

questions.q: Where do SSD and magnetic HDD sit relative to memory on the speed/cost scale, and where is bulk data stored?
questions.answer: SSDs sit closer to memory in speed and cost; magnetic HDDs are slower but much cheaper. Huge amounts of data are stored on magnetic disks, not SSDs.

questions.q: How does a read on a magnetic disk physically happen, and what is the most time-consuming part?
questions.answer: A file byte offset is translated to a disk, sector and offset; the platter spins and the head moves to that location, reads it and passes data to the device driver and user space. The mechanical movement (head seek and rotation) is the most time-consuming part.

questions.q: When a student suggested a memtable/SSTable, what requirement did the teacher clarify?
questions.answer: A PUT must be persisted immediately - flushed to disk at once, not buffered in memory.

questions.q: How are PUTs done, and why is that the best one can do on a magnetic disk?
questions.answer: Append every put to the end of an append-only file, no matter what. The head is already where the last write ended, so there is zero seek and no big mechanical movement.

questions.q: After PUT K1 V1, K2 V2, K3 V3, a PUT K1 V1' arrives. What happens in the file?
questions.answer: K1 V1' is appended as a new entry at the end; the old K1 V1 is not changed - you never go back to find and modify it.

questions.q: Why can't a delete just overwrite the key's old value with a special value?
questions.answer: It is an append-only file: you may read earlier positions but you cannot write to any earlier location.

questions.q: How is DEL K2 implemented, and what does that give?
questions.answer: DEL K2 = PUT(K2, -1): append an entry for K2 with a special value (tombstone, e.g. -1). Delete becomes as cheap (O(1)) as a put.

questions.q: What is the naive GET on the append-only file and how is it made fast?
questions.answer: Naive: scan all entries and return the latest one for the key (slow). Fast: an in-memory hash table mapping key -> offset of its latest entry in the file (offset only, not the value), updated on every append.

questions.q: Which kind of access does an append-only file allow and forbid?
questions.answer: Random reads are allowed; random writes are not (writes only at the end).

questions.q: Walk through the in-memory hash table for PUT K1 V1, PUT K2 V2, PUT K3 V3, PUT K1 V1', DEL K2.
questions.answer: Write to disk first, then update memory: K1->O1, K2->O2, K3->O3; K1 V1' appended at O4 so K1->O4; DEL K2 appends the tombstone and removes K2 from the hash table. Final: K1->O4, K3->O3, no K2.

questions.q: What is the GET flow, and what happens after a machine crash wipes the in-memory hash table?
questions.answer: GET: look up the key in the hash table; absent -> 404; present -> go to the offset in the file and read the value. After a crash, on restart iterate through the whole file and rebuild the index (slower recovery accepted).

questions.q: What limitation comes from keeping the index in memory?
questions.answer: The number of keys is bounded by RAM: all keys (with their offsets) must fit in memory; values live on disk.

questions.q: Why can't the single append-only file just grow forever? Give the reasons discussed, including the one the teacher called biggest.
questions.answer: The disk runs out of space since stale/deleted entries are never reclaimed; one huge file is slow to rebuild/scan. Biggest: file system limitations - the file system may not support files beyond a certain size (e.g. 1 TB; BTRFS, NTFS have limits).

questions.q: A student proposed splitting a 100 TB disk into 10 TB files. What did the teacher suggest instead?
questions.answer: Keep smaller files, e.g. 100 MB or 1 GB; as soon as the size threshold is crossed, start writing to a new file. This is file rotation.

questions.q: With file rotation, which files take writes and reads, and what must the in-memory index now store?
questions.answer: Only one file (e.g. 004) is active and receives all writes; all older files are read-only/immutable but still readable. The index must store which file and the offset (e.g. K1 -> f1, O4).

questions.q: What does merge and compaction do, and what must happen afterwards?
questions.answer: Take the read-only files, iterate through them and write a new combined file that skips stale (overwritten) and deleted entries; then delete the old files forever. Because offsets change, the in-memory index must be updated (atomically) for moved entries.

questions.q: What shape does disk usage take over time with merge and compaction, and what line bounds it?
questions.answer: A sawtooth: usage grows as writes come in, then drops sharply when merge and compaction runs, repeating. It must never cross the disk capacity cap (e.g. 1 TB), or the system crashes.

questions.q: What two configuration parameters does the store expose, how do you tune them, and what goes wrong at either extreme?
questions.answer: (1) Merge-and-compaction frequency; (2) file rotation threshold (file size). Tune by monitoring the sawtooth. Too frequent: too much garbage-collection work, CPU starved of real work. Too infrequent: work accumulates and usage can breach disk capacity.

questions.q: Does this append-only design give the same benefit on SSDs?
questions.answer: No. SSDs still benefit but not as significantly, since they use flash memory, not a spinning disk, and already handle writes well. On cheap magnetic disks it gives near-SSD speed (prepared notes: high write throughput even on HDD, '5000x gain'; 'the SSD does not give similar gain').

questions.q: Why is 'read until newline' a bad way to read a record from disk?
questions.answer: Keys and values are variable length; reading byte by byte until '\n' means many disk I/Os, very slow. Files are read in blocks; you must know exactly how many bytes to read to get the whole entry in one shot.

questions.q: How do key size and value size fields make reads predictable? Give the field sizes and the number of disk I/Os.
questions.answer: Each record starts with KSZ (4-byte int) and VSZ (4-byte int). Read those 8 bytes first (one I/O), then read KSZ + VSZ bytes in one more I/O and split into key and value. Same idea applies to the dictionary (word size, meaning size).

questions.q: What failure motivates integrity checks in the record, and why is reading such a record dangerous?
questions.answer: The machine crashes while writing a large value (e.g. only '110' written). The data is lost and can't be fixed, but you must detect it: reading VSZ bytes would run into the next entry and serve corrupt data.

questions.q: What is the CRC, what does it cover, and why is it placed first (leftmost)? Give the real examples cited.
questions.answer: A cyclic redundancy check: a checksum/hash over key size, value size, key and value, computed in memory before writing. It is the first thing written/flushed because it is the minimum needed to detect corruption (you can't put it at the end). Postgres commit log and MySQL binlog put CRC leftmost; network formats send it first.

questions.q: Give the final record layout, left to right, and what the TS field is for.
questions.answer: CRC | TS | KSZ | VSZ | K | V. TS is a timestamp used for conflicts.

questions.q: How are partial writes handled when reading a record or compacting?
questions.answer: If the first (header) write fails, the entry simply doesn't exist. If the header lands but the key/value write fails, the CRC won't match on read, so tell the user the entry is corrupted - never serve corrupt data. Recovery is mostly heuristic: ignore the entry in merge and compaction, as if the write never happened.

questions.q: With multiple files, what does an in-memory index entry hold (prepared notes), and what three steps make a GET?
questions.answer: Key -> File ID | VSZ (entry size) | VPOS (offset) | TS (timestamp). GET: hash table lookup, disk seek, disk read (a pointed query); the index points at the latest entry for the key.

questions.q: Why is merging Bitcask's files different from merging the dictionary with its changelog?
questions.answer: Bitcask files are not sorted (entries in arrival order), so it is not a merge-sort merge; instead load entries into a temporary hash table, replacing older entries with later ones and dropping deleted keys, then flush to disk without stale or deleted entries.

questions.q: List the limitation and the strengths of the designed DB as given.
questions.answer: Limitation: keys must fit in memory. Strengths: O(1) reads, writes, deletes; high write throughput and low latency (bare minimum disk I/O); I/O saturation (the device does real work, max out of the hardware); easy backups (just copy the files).

questions.q: What is the database just designed called, and what kind of database is it?
questions.answer: Bitcask. It is an embedded database (a library, like SQLite), not a central server that clients connect to.

questions.q: How is Bitcask used in production according to the lecture, and what analogy was given?
questions.answer: Riak, a key-value store, uses Bitcask as its backend; Uber uses Riak in production for its main ride-hailing service. Riak makes Bitcask distributed (proxy/routing, consistent hashing, replication, consensus, data movement), each Riak node running a Bitcask instance - like Elasticsearch is an HTTP/distributed wrapper over Lucene.

questions.q: What claim did the teacher make about any system advertising high throughput with persistence?
questions.answer: It must be using an append-only file or something similar; otherwise it isn't truly high-throughput.

questions.q: What did the teacher recommend doing with Bitcask, and how should it be benchmarked?
questions.answer: Implement it yourself (read the Bitcask paper too), spending about a week; benchmark it against on-disk and in-memory KV stores on HDDs and SSDs, monitoring with Prometheus to see I/O saturate.

questions.q: How does Bitcask differ from SSTables/memtables (LSM trees), per the Q&A?
questions.answer: SSTables/memtables keep values (sorted) in memory and buffer writes before flushing, so data can be lost if memory goes down; Bitcask keeps only keys and offsets in memory and persists every write immediately to disk. SSTables are covered next week; Bitcask is the foundation for them.

questions.q: How do you create an append-only file in practice - do you preallocate e.g. 1 GB?
questions.answer: No. Open the file with the append mode option 'a' (vs r, w, r+, w+) and just write; the file system (BTRFS, NTFS, ext2/3/4) handles block allocation, typically reserving decent free space so the file can grow.

questions.q: How are tombstoned (deleted) keys handled during merge and compaction?
questions.answer: While merging the immutable files (not the active one), buffer key-value pairs in a temporary hash table, replacing older values; a deleted key is removed from that table; then flush it as the new file. Stale and deleted entries are never copied. This temporary hash table is separate from the in-memory index.

questions.q: A student asked whether writing the CRC/header is atomic while the large value is not, given kernels differ. What was the answer?
questions.answer: The small header part (CRC, timestamp, key size, value size - roughly 20 bytes) is written first and will definitely land; the kernel may not guarantee atomicity of a big value. More paranoid systems keep a separate WAL.

questions.q: Why did the teacher choose a 1 TB size for a 170,000-word dictionary?
questions.answer: To make it impossible to copy the dictionary onto every API server, forcing the discussion of cost, network attached storage and portability. To justify it, imagine meanings include multimedia (audio, video, visualizations).

questions.q: Is one S3 read per API request expensive? What did the teacher say about S3's cost and latency for this pattern?
questions.answer: In a real service you would add caching etc. The point was that pointed reads on S3 are possible, enabling cold storage. S3/network I/O are not free and S3 is slow, but storage is very cheap, so it fits infrequent reads where higher latency is fine.

questions.q: What point did the teacher make about 'MB' when reflecting on the index size?
questions.answer: We treat MBs lightly, but M means a million bytes: the small index still holds a lot of information; the example shows how small an index can be relative to the data.

questions.q: In a rolling redeployment, does the load balancer change, and do you have to write code for it?
questions.answer: The LB stays; servers are removed and replaced one at a time. Rolling deployment is given out of the box by the cloud provider - no code needed; just make a call to trigger a deployment.

questions.q: Are index offsets line numbers, and what exactly does the header's index-size field store?
questions.answer: Offsets are byte positions where the record starts, not line numbers. The header stores the actual number of bytes of the index stored in the file (not a path to a separate file): read the header, get the index size, read that many bytes as the index, then serve from the data.

questions.q: Since the index size changes with updates, how does the header stay correct?
questions.answer: Each weekly merge creates an entirely new file: new dictionary data, new index and a new header.

questions.q: Why keep the dictionary sorted, and what is the merge complexity as a result?
questions.answer: Lookups use the index, so sorting is not needed for reads; but sorted dictionary + sorted changelog make the merge a single pass, O(n), instead of O(n^2), and the new file is sorted for next week too. 'Computer science is obsessed with sorted data.'
